content: Scombroid poisoning is a foodborne illness that occurs after consuming seafood that has been improperly stored. It is the second most common type of seafood poisoning, following ciguatera poisoning. However, it is frequently misdiagnosed because its symptoms mimic those of an allergic reaction. Unlike many other forms of food poisoning, scombroid poisoning is not caused by an organism or virus. Instead, it results from the natural presence of histidine in certain fish species. When these fish are stored at temperatures above 60 degrees Fahrenheit, histidine is converted into histamine, a biogenic amine. This is why it is critical to store fish at low temperatures. Histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures, meaning that even properly cooked fish can still cause poisoning. Since histamine is a mediator of allergic reactions, the symptoms of scombroid poisoning resemble those seen in severe allergic responses. The symptoms of scombroid poisoning include skin flushing, a throbbing headache, a burning sensation in the mouth, abdominal cramps, nausea, diarrhea, palpitations, a sense of unease, and, in rare cases, prostration or temporary loss of vision. These symptoms typically appear within 10 to 30 minutes of consuming the affected fish and are generally self-limiting. Physical signs may include diffuse blanching erythema, tachycardia, wheezing, and either hypotension or hypertension. Individuals with asthma are at greater risk of experiencing respiratory complications, such as wheezing or bronchospasms. Treatment for scombroid poisoning primarily involves supportive care, including the administration of fluids and oxygen. Medications that block H1 and H2 histamine receptors can also be used with some success to alleviate symptoms.
